hook: An organization can apologize fluently while leaving the machinery that caused the harm intact.
readerPromise: Investigate institutional harm through the relationship between distributed responsibility, incentives and moral self-description.
protectedRevelations: Later historical verdicts and proposed corrective architectures
visualPlan: The apology and the machinery: Show a fluent apology beside the unchanged control that continues the harmful operation. Keep the organization's reassuring statement and its repeated consequences in the same frame.

Many roles, one consequence: Pass one decision through clinician, office and management desks without giving any person the whole view. Let a person affected by the decision remain visible beside the institution's caring public statement.

Where responsibility disappears: Follow the decision record as each role passes responsibility onward. Place observable actions and records on the review desk rather than drawing a hidden institutional mind.

What does the institution notice?: Repeat the same harmful output after the apology, without melodrama or graphic harm. End on the outside report next to the institution's own account, leaving the contradiction visible.

cueChanges.nextVisualChange: Keep the public apology beside an unchanged operational process, without sinister facial caricatures.
Show a consequence passing through three distinct roles while keeping the affected person in view.
Use the existing responsibility documents to reveal a gap rather than naming a single invented villain.
Close with the institution’s ordinary record and the reader’s question about what activates correction.

sentenceIntentions.text: An organization can apologize fluently while leaving the machinery that caused the harm intact.
sentenceIntentions.purpose: Contrast fluent apology with unchanged harmful operation
sentenceIntentions.viewerResponse: Recognize institutional conscience as potentially performative

sentenceIntentions.text: Egregopathy names a recurring pattern: an organization keeps harming people while telling a convincing story about its goodness.
sentenceIntentions.purpose: Define egregopathy as repeated harm beside convincing moral self-description
sentenceIntentions.viewerResponse: Recognize the proposed pattern without imagining a hidden collective mind

sentenceIntentions.text: A hospital, a bank, and a platform coordinate many decisions that no single participant sees whole.
sentenceIntentions.purpose: Make distributed decisions concrete across three institutions
sentenceIntentions.viewerResponse: See why no one participant experiences the whole

sentenceIntentions.text: The book asks how organizations can treat people as tools while still presenting themselves as caring and fair.
sentenceIntentions.purpose: Show people becoming instruments under respectable self-description
sentenceIntentions.viewerResponse: Feel the human stakes beneath procedure

sentenceIntentions.text: Responsibility becomes harder to locate as decisions pass through separate roles, rules, and rewards.
sentenceIntentions.purpose: Track responsibility across roles and incentives

sentenceIntentions.text: The proposed term names patterns people can inspect, without imagining a hidden mind inside an organization.
sentenceIntentions.purpose: Keep the proposed term grounded in observable patterns

sentenceIntentions.text: An apology starts to sound different when the same harm has become part of ordinary procedure.
sentenceIntentions.purpose: Connect the inquiry with routine institutional betrayal
sentenceIntentions.viewerResponse: Expect analysis of how harm persists

sentenceIntentions.text: Begin with the institution seen from outside, and ask which harms its own story leaves out.
sentenceIntentions.purpose: Ask which harms reach the organization's own account
sentenceIntentions.viewerResponse: Want to examine what its apology leaves untouched

distinctiveContribution: Egregopathy is proposed as a functional name for institutions repeatedly turning people into instruments while retaining a convincing moral self-description.
